blocks.text: Psychological support is important to cope with this chronic illness.
Hypo-hyper glycemia education needs to be reinforce frequently.
Step 1 Calculate total daily insulin need, generally 0.3 to 1unit/kg/day initially, after honeymoon period its between 0.7-
1.5units/kg/day. However individual patient needs should be considered.
Basal insulin: Long acting(analogs) or NPH (intermediate acting)
Bolus insulin: Regular(soluble) or Rapid acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine)
Estimated dose is adjusted depending on the child’s response
Basal long-acting insulin analog: dose is 40%-50% the TDD, give 24 hourly in the evening
Basal NPH: two thirds of TDD before breakfast, one third before dinner or at bedtime.

Usually, 50% of the total dose, the dose of insulin given depends on the anticipated carbohydrates, premeal BG as well as exercise activity. Total premeal bolus is the sum of the dose calculated based on ICR plus dose adjusted to correct premeal hyperglycemia. ICR (amount of carbohydrate (grams) covered by 1unit of insulin=450/TDD

Pre-mixed insulins not advised in children

blocks.text: Correct perioperative management depends on type of surgery (major or minor), type of diabetes and recent diabetes control. A perioperative HBA1c, fasting or random blood glucose is recommended to assess glycemic control and identify undiagnosed diabetes
Surgery should be delayed if possible if HBA1C >9% or blood glucose fasting >10 mmol/l or random glucose > 13 mmol/l.
Screen for nephropathy, cardiac disease, retinopathy and neuropathy and inform surgical team.
Optimal glycemic target in the perioperative period should be to maintain blood glucose levels between 7.8-10mmol/l
If diabetes is well controlled and surgery is minor:
If on oral agent therapy, omit therapy on morning of surgery except SGLTS2 inhibitors which should be stopped 24 to 72hour before surgery and resume therapy when eating normally

runs.text: If on oral agent therapy, omit therapy on morning of surgery except SGLTS2 inhibitors which should be stopped 24 to 72hour before surgery and resume therapy when eating normally

blocks.text: For T1DM, continue with normal basal dose of insulin, the short acting or rapid acting insulins can be given as per correctional scale insulin.

Decrease the dose of long-acting basal insulin by 20% to 25% the evening before surgery. If they routinely take basal insulin only in the morning, the reduced dose should instead be administered on the morning of surgery.

runs.text: Decrease the dose of long-acting basal insulin by 20% to 25% the evening before surgery. If they routinely take basal insulin only in the morning, the reduced dose should instead be administered on the morning of surgery.

blocks.text: In cases of intermediate-acting insulin such as neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH), the usual dose is administered the evening prior and reduced by 50% on the morning of surgery.

blocks.text: Patients using premixed insulin (NPH/regular 70/30) should preferably receive long-acting insulin the evening before surgery instead of their premixed formulation. Or reduce the premixed insulin dose by 50%

blocks.text: Pre-prandial insulin should be stopped; subcutaneous correctional insulin is initiated with blood glucose monitoring every 4 to 6 hours
If poor glycemic control or major surgery:
Use continuous IV insulin infusion, start with half of the patient’s usual total daily dose (TDD usually 0.4 to 0.5 U/kg/day) or 1-5 units of regular insulin per hour.

runs.text: U/kg/day) or 1-5 units of regular insulin per hour.

blocks.text: Monitor blood glucose before, during and after surgery as outlined below: aim for blood glucose levels of 7.8–10 mmol/l.
Check potassium levels and start potassium infusion as per DKA protocol
Infuse 0.9% NaCl with D5W IV at 50 mL/hr.
Adjusting infusion rate according to blood sugar levels, if blood glucose (BG) is:

< 4mmol/l: stop insulin infusion, administer D50% 50mls iv push stat, continue D 5%infusion at 50ml/hr, monitor blood glucose every 30min, restart insulin at half the initial rate when blood glucose >10mmol/l

blocks.text: Management of Diabetes during Religious Fasting
There are several types of fasting:
Normal fast (the common fast): the person abstains from all foods but can take water for a limited time. Or abstain from food and water for a specific number of hours during the day.

runs.text: from food and water for a specific number of hours during the day.

blocks.text: Total fast = total abstinence from both food and water. This should not go beyond a maximum of three days and is not recommended for those people taking insulin secretagogues or insulin.

runs.text: Total fast = total abstinence from both food and water.
This should not go beyond a maximum of three days and is not recommended for those people taking insulin secretagogues or insulin.

blocks.text: Partial fast = abstain from selected foods and drinks, or omit a certain meal each of the fasting days.
